name: Lena Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the injection moulding presses at a plastics plant out on the ring road industrial estate. We make clips and vent housings for car makers, little grey bits you'd never notice in your dashboard. I run two presses a shift: I watch the cycle, pull samples, check them against the gauge, clear jams and box the good parts. The noise and the heat off the barrels wear you out, and on nights your eyes go funny from staring at the same grey plastic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and who do you spend the day with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a run goes clean for hours and the boxes stack up and nobody shouts. I eat lunch with Dorota from the next line, we've done that for eleven years, always the same bench by the vending machine. Last year they put a robot arm on press 6 that takes the parts out and drops them on a belt, and Pieter who used to do that went onto permanent nights. I've never touched a computer at work beyond the press screen, and I'd like to keep it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for years, it's a lot of noise from people who've never stood next to a press. At the union meeting I'd probably make a joke about it. I'm not online much, my partner Mark does the internet in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my problem. The robot arm on press 6 isn't clever, it just grabs and drops, and it came in without any of this AI talk. So hype or no hype, the arms keep creeping along the line one press at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep doing my shifts and say yes to every Saturday they offer. I'd keep going to the union branch meetings on the first Tuesday, because that's where we heard about press 6 before management told us. We've got about nine hundred in the account at the best of times, so overtime is the only cushion I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, I suppose, that the big scary version isn't coming. But the money worry was there before AI and it'll be there after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robot arm on press 6. Would that keep spreading even in this picture, where AI fizzles out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time the machine goes down, I'm the one they call. I'm not worried about this AI, I'm worried about the next arm, and whether they put it on my press or Dorota's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In an ordinary year like that, which bill worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, every time. It's eleven years old and if the clutch goes, I can't get to the estate, there's no bus at six in the morning. After that it's Mia's school trip money, and I hate saying no to her.

S0.say: It's a lot of noise from people who've never stood next to a press. I'd probably make a joke about it at the union meeting.
S0.think: Hype or not, it doesn't change my real problem, because simple robot arms are already spreading along the line. The press 6 arm came in without any AI talk at all.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts and takes every Saturday overtime offered, since about nine hundred in the account is her only buffer. Keeps going to the monthly union branch meeting to hear early about new machines.
S0.feel: Some relief that the big version isn't coming, but the money worry she already had stays exactly where it was.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about this AI, I'm worried about the next arm, and whether they put it on my press or Dorota's.
S0.fieldNote: Lena separates AI from robots very sharply: to her the threat is the plain robot arm, which is already here. Even in the calmest picture her mood is set by a thin bank balance and a car she can't afford to lose. The union branch is her early-warning system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it has to be negotiated, full stop. Nobody gets dumped, there's a retraining fund, and the people on the floor get a say in which machines come in. I'd say that at the branch and I'd say it to the plant manager's face if I got the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is exactly the kind that goes. I'm not the setter, I don't change the moulds or fix the hydraulics, I watch and clear and box. If they offer retraining it'll be on a computer, and I'm slow on those, so the younger ones will get the new jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get a written agreement before the next machines are ordered, not after. At home we'd cut Jonas's swimming club and the phone contracts this year, and I'd stop buying lunch from the van. If the company ran a course I'd sign up, but I'd want Dorota next to me, I'm not doing it on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly, and angry under it. Angry that it's always us who have to change and never the people who own the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost your shifts in this picture, how would the household manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's job in the care home kitchen is safer than mine, I think, but it pays even less. If I lost my shifts we'd be on his wage and whatever the state gives, and the mortgage alone is more than half of his pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia and Jonas if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kids the truth, roughly. Mia's thirteen, she'd see through anything. I'd say Mum's job is changing and we're going to be careful with money for a while, and that's not their fault.

S1.say: It has to be negotiated: nobody gets dumped, there's a retraining fund and people on the floor get a say in which machines come in. She'd say it at the union branch and to the plant manager.
S1.think: Her job is exactly the kind that goes, because she watches, clears and boxes rather than setting moulds. Any retraining will likely be computer-based and the younger workers will get the new jobs first.
S1.do: Pushes the union branch to win a written agreement before new machines are ordered. Cuts her son's swimming club, the phone contracts and bought lunches this year, and signs up for a company course only alongside her friend Dorota.
S1.feel: Scared, with anger underneath that workers always have to change and owners never do.
S1.quote: Angry that it's always us who have to change and never the people who own the place.
S1.fieldNote: Lena's public line is about fairness and process, while privately she already sees herself at the back of the queue for any new role. She would only take on a course with a friend beside her, which says a lot about how she handles change. She still feels the union gives her some control here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they should stop it, or at least slow it down by law until people are looked after. I'd be at every rally the union called. I don't care if that sounds old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is nothing. The plant would order the robots before the ink was dry and there'd be nothing for me on the estate, the tile works already shut. I don't see what I do. I really don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't the mortgage, food and the car. I'd go to the bank with Mark and ask about freezing the mortgage before we missed anything, and I'd find out what benefits we could claim. I'd march, I'd vote for whoever promised to protect people, and I'd ask my sister if we could move in with her if the house went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I picture sitting at the kitchen table with the letter and Mia watching me read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say: retrain fast. What do you make of that, with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn what? If the machine can do almost anything a person can do, what am I going to learn in two years with no money that it can't do better? I'm not being stubborn, I just can't see the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dorota, because she's on her own with her boy. And the older men on the night shift who've done nothing else since school. Pieter's fifty-five, who's going to take him on?

S2.say: They should stop it, or slow it by law until people are looked after, and she'd be at every union rally. She doesn't mind if that sounds old-fashioned.
S2.think: Two years is nothing: the plant would order robots straight away and there's nothing else on the estate since the tile works shut. She can't see what she would do.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except mortgage, food and the car, and goes to the bank with Mark to ask about freezing the mortgage before missing a payment. Claims what benefits she can, joins rallies, votes for protection and asks her sister about moving in.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone, picturing reading the letter at the kitchen table with her daughter watching.
S2.quote: If the machine can do almost anything a person can do, what am I going to learn in two years with no money that it can't do better?
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Lena with no plan she believes in, and she says so plainly; her actions are all about holding on to the house. She rejects retraining not out of stubbornness, as she puts it, but because she can't see a door. Her concern quickly turns to Dorota and older night-shift colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for anyone in charge to be caught out. The union should be at the table now, demanding a proper plan for every plant on the estate. Online I'd probably share the union's posts, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends with me out of a job, just later. The difference is Jonas would be fourteen instead of eleven, and maybe the mortgage would be a bit smaller. But I'd spend five years waiting for it, which might be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd try to put something away every month, even if it's fifty, and I'd stop the credit card for good. I'd go to the branch and ask to be on the committee, which I've always said no to. And I'd make sure Mia picks a subject at school that's about people, nursing or teaching, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying something you can't put down for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the committee. What would make you actually do that, when you haven't before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I said I'd go on the committee, and I mean it. I've sat at the back for fifteen years. If it's coming in five years I'd rather be the one asking the questions than the one reading the notice board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're steering Mia towards people jobs, but the card says AGI could do almost any work. Is that a guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. If AGI can do the nursing too, then I'm guessing like everyone else. I just think people will want a person holding their hand longer than they'll want a person boxing clips.

S3.say: With five years there's no excuse for anyone in charge to be caught out, and the union should be at the table now demanding a plan for every plant on the estate. Online she'd share the union's posts.
S3.think: It still ends with her out of work, only later, with the children a bit older and the mortgage a bit smaller. Five years of waiting for it might be worse than two.
S3.do: Puts away even fifty a month and stops using the credit card. Finally joins the union branch committee after years of saying no, and steers her daughter towards a people-focused subject like nursing or teaching.
S3.feel: Heavy, like carrying something she can't put down for five years.
S3.quote: If it's coming in five years I'd rather be the one asking the questions than the one reading the notice board.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make Lena feel safer, but it moves her from the back of the room to the committee. She admits her advice to Mia is a guess. The idea of waiting five years for a known blow seems almost as bad to her as getting it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so if people get hurt, it's because someone chose that. I'd want the government to fund it, the transition, I mean, out of what these companies make. That's what I'd say at the branch and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years changes a lot for me. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown and out, Mia would be twenty-three. The mortgage would be close to done. I'd still lose the job, but I wouldn't be dragging two children down with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep my head down, and put as much as I could into paying off the mortgage early. I'd stay on the union committee and go to the regional meetings about it, and vote for whoever puts money behind people, not machines. I wouldn't retrain for something new, I'd be honest about that, I'd ride the press out as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but still a knot in my stomach. Ten years goes fast when you're counting mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not retrain, with a full ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know myself. I've watched the young lads learn the new screen in an afternoon and it took me a month. In ten years I'd rather spend my energy making sure there's money for people like me at the end than pretending I'll be a programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could only get one thing done in those ten years, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying the house off. If I own the roof over my head when the press goes quiet, I can live on very little. Everything else comes second to that.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so if people get hurt it's because someone chose that. The government should fund the transition from what the companies make.
S4.think: Ten years changes a lot: she'd be 53, the children grown and the mortgage nearly done. She'd still lose the job but wouldn't drag two children down with her.
S4.do: Keeps working and pays extra off the mortgage wherever she can, aiming to own the house before the press goes quiet. Stays on the union committee, goes to regional meetings and votes for parties that fund people through the change.
S4.feel: Calmer than the other pictures, but with a knot in her stomach because ten years goes fast when you're counting mortgage payments.
S4.quote: If I own the roof over my head when the press goes quiet, I can live on very little.
S4.fieldNote: For Lena the decade matters mainly because her children will be grown and her mortgage nearly paid. She is frank that she won't retrain and would rather put her energy into the union and paying off the house. Her plan is to hold on, not to reinvent herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is time and money together: wages kept for a year or two while things settle, and the mortgage frozen, not just a leaflet about courses. And the union in the room when they decide which machines come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'm proud of. I've put two kids through school on press money and never missed a payment. Whatever happens with these robots, I'd like somebody to remember that the people on the line held things together.

headlineQuote: I've put two kids through school on press money and never missed a payment.
portrait: Lena Weber is 43 and runs two injection moulding presses at a car-parts plastics plant, living with her partner Mark, a care home cook, and their two children on about nine hundred in the bank. She has never used AI and doesn't plan to, and to her the real threat is the plain robot arm already working on press 6. She leans on the union and is quick to name owners and government as the people who should carry the cost. She is uneasy even in the calm picture, panicked at two years, and only steadies at ten years because by then her children will be grown and the mortgage nearly paid. Across every picture her plan is to hold on rather than reinvent herself.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because the plant would buy robots immediately and there is no other work on the estate.
whatWouldHelp: Wages kept for a year or two and the mortgage frozen, rather than leaflets about courses, plus the union in the room when new machines are chosen.
